02 / SELECTED CASE

FOOTWEAR PRODUCT TESTING · THREE-PHASE STORY

From controlled testing
to engineering judgment.

A progression from cushioning comparison to traction-data review and follow-up validation. I applied existing methods, checked results against test conditions, and communicated what the data could—and could not—support.

PHASE 1 · MECHANICAL TESTING

Forefoot Impulse · Midsole comparison

Applied the existing method to six requested development-midsole configurations at a 2,000 N target. Compared Energy Input/Return, Efficiency, Penetration, Max Load, and Stiffness.

6configurations compared
1,997–2,001 Nmeasured maximum-load values
13.1–18.3 mmpenetration range
106–149 N/mmstiffness range

One reported result per condition. Differences describe measured response across tested configurations; they do not establish repeatability or causal fixture effects.

PHASE 2 · TRACTION TEST

Compared six development footwear configurations against one benchmark under a 1,000 N traction condition. Reviewed DCOF together with actual load, force channels, surface velocity, and shoe side.

THE UNEXPECTED RESULT

A blocker-added prototype on the left showed mean DCOF 1.80 with mean actual-load magnitude 703.53 N—296.47 N (29.65%) below target. The higher DCOF was not treated as “best traction” without checking load comparability.

PHASE 3 · FOLLOW-UP VALIDATION

Reviewed laced and unlaced conditions by shoe side, comparing load, speed, and friction data. Considered construction, blocker/midsole, sample thickness, compression, shoe fixation, and return movement as potential contributors.

ENGINEERING RECOMMENDATION

Proposed a project-level ±5% actual-load review window around 1,000 N to support data-validity assessment. This was a study proposal, not an official company standard; follow-up run count is omitted pending source-record reconciliation.

PROGRESSION Controlled comparison → anomaly detection → load validity check → controlled follow-up → bounded technical recommendation.

03 / TOOLS & PROCESS

TEST DATA VISUALIZATION

Keep analysis moving
when a system is down.

When a data-platform integration issue interrupted test-result visualization, I planned and built an Excel VBA tool to keep the analysis workflow moving.

2CSV sources imported and consolidated
4metrics calculated per sample
2chart types generated automatically
~10 minfrom raw data to dashboard output

The tool imports Tracking and Trends CSVs, calculates Energy Return, Energy Efficiency, Stiffness, and Penetration at Cycle 100, then generates sample comparisons, load-deflection curves, and a dashboard.
